clinicalPearls: An autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease defined by linear deposition of IgA along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence — the diagnostic hallmark.

Has two peaks: a childhood form (chronic bullous disease of childhood) and an adult form; the childhood pattern classically shows annular or polycyclic lesions with peripheral blisters — the 'cluster of jewels' or 'string of pearls' sign.

Childhood lesions favour the lower abdomen, perineum, genitals, buttocks and inner thighs, and are often perioral; adult disease is more variable and may mimic bullous pemphigoid or dermatitis herpetiformis.
Drug-induced disease is well recognised, with vancomycin the classic culprit; other reported triggers include some antibiotics, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors.
Target antigens are cleavage fragments of the ectodomain of collagen XVII/BP180 (termed LAD-1 and LABD97) located within the lamina lucida.
Unlike dermatitis herpetiformis, it is NOT associated with coeliac disease or gluten sensitivity, so a gluten-free diet is not indicated.
Mucosal involvement can occur, including scarring conjunctivitis that resembles mucous membrane pemphigoid.
Dapsone is the usual first-line therapy (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status should be checked first), and drug-induced cases typically resolve after withdrawal of the offending agent.
reference.pathophysiology: Linear IgA disease is caused by IgA autoantibodies directed against antigens in the cutaneous basement membrane zone, predominantly proteolytically processed fragments of the ectodomain of collagen XVII (BP180), known as LAD-1 and LABD97, which reside within the lamina lucida. Deposition of IgA along the dermo-epidermal junction activates complement and recruits neutrophils, whose released proteases and reactive species degrade adhesion structures and split the epidermis from the dermis, producing tense subepidermal blisters. Histologically this generates a subepidermal blister with a neutrophil-rich infiltrate and neutrophilic microabscesses in the dermal papillae, features that can closely mimic dermatitis herpetiformis. The disease may be idiopathic or drug-induced, with vancomycin the archetypal precipitant, and it can affect skin and mucous membranes. Crucially, unlike dermatitis herpetiformis it is not linked to gluten-sensitive enteropathy, reflecting a different antigenic target and immunopathological mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Erythema multiforme or Stevens-Johnson syndrome in acute severe presentations
In children: bullous impetigo and scabies
additionalInvestigations: Lesional skin biopsy (subepidermal blister with a neutrophil-rich infiltrate and papillary microabscesses)
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showing homogeneous linear IgA at the basement membrane zone
Indirect immunofluorescence including salt-split skin (binding typically to the epidermal/roof side)
Immunoblot or ELISA for BP180-related antigens
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase assay before starting dapsone
Detailed drug history, particularly for recent vancomycin
Ophthalmology and mucosal assessment if mucosal symptoms are present
redFlags: Ocular involvement with conjunctival scarring or symblepharon, carrying a risk of blindness and requiring ophthalmology input
Laryngeal or pharyngeal mucosal disease threatening the airway
Recent vancomycin or other suspect drug as a potentially reversible trigger
reference.prognosis: The childhood form is frequently self-limiting, often remitting spontaneously within a few years or around puberty, whereas adult idiopathic disease tends to be more chronic though usually controllable. Drug-induced disease generally resolves after withdrawal of the causative agent.
pitfalls: Confusing it with dermatitis herpetiformis and wrongly imposing a lifelong gluten-free diet.
Diagnosing on histology alone without direct immunofluorescence, which is the definitive test.
Missing a drug trigger such as vancomycin.
Overlooking mucosal or ocular disease and its scarring potential.
Starting dapsone without first checking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status.
